title: BUG: composed DateOffset rejected on the array path (GH#66549)
body:
Addresses one item from GH-66549 (the second half of item 2); the rest of that issue stays open.

Adding a `DateOffset` that has both a month/year component and a timedelta component to a `DatetimeIndex` or `Series` raised for a result the scalar path returns:

```python
>>> pd.Timestamp.max + pd.DateOffset(months=1, days=-31)
Timestamp('2262-04-10 23:47:16.854775807')
>>> pd.DatetimeIndex([pd.Timestamp.max]) + pd.DateOffset(months=1, days=-31)
OutOfBoundsDatetime: Out of bounds nanosecond timestamp: 2262-05-11 23:47:16
```

`RelativeDeltaOffset._apply_array` materialized the month-shifted intermediate as datetime64 before adding the timedelta component, so a representable final result was rejected because a transient value was not.

`_shift_months_and_add` now applies both components in one pass. The month shift leaves the time-of-day alone, so it accumulates the date part in days — where no pandas-representable value can overflow — folds in the offset's whole-day part, and only then converts the result date to the target resolution. The reso-matching in `_add_timedelta_overflowsafe` is factored out into `_match_reso` so both paths promote identically. Offsets with no timedelta component, and the other `shift_months` callers, keep the existing code path.

A result landing within the first day of the bottom of the range still raises, since that day's start is itself unrepresentable. That is unchanged from the current behavior.

title: API: astype to CategoricalDtype matches by lookup instead of casting, so legitimate casts silently become NaN
body:
`astype` to a `CategoricalDtype` resolves values by *lookup* rather than by *cast*: `Categorical.__init__` ends up in `_get_codes_for_values`, which does `categories.get_indexer_for(values)`. When the values are perfectly representable in `categories.dtype` but are currently stored in a different dtype, every lookup misses and the result is silently all-NaN.

### Reproducible Example

No pyarrow, no datetimes — just int values against string categories, and vice versa:

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

pd.Series([1, 2]).astype(pd.CategoricalDtype(pd.Index(["1", "2"], dtype="str")))
# 0    NaN
# 1    NaN
# dtype: category
# Categories (2, str): ['1', '2']

# the two-step cast, which is what the user meant:
pd.Categorical(pd.Series([1, 2]).astype("str"),
               dtype=pd.CategoricalDtype(pd.Index(["1", "2"], dtype="str")))
# ['1', '2']
# Categories (2, str): [1, 2]
```

```python
pd.Series(np.array(["1", "2"], dtype=object)).astype(pd.CategoricalDtype(pd.Index([1, 2])))
# 0    NaN
# 1    NaN
# dtype: category
# Categories (2, int64): [1, 2]
```

Both emit `Pandas4Warning: Constructing a Categorical with a dtype and values containing non-null entries not in that dtype's categories is deprecated and will raise in a future version.` — but the values *are* in the categories. Only the dtype differs.

### Why this needs a decision now

The deprecation added in GH-62142 will turn all of these into a hard error. Its two motivating issues, GH-40996 and GH-59899, are both about values that are *genuinely absent* from the categories (`pd.Categorical(["foo"], dtype=ci.dtype)`, `"c"` against `["a", "b"]`), and raising there is clearly right.

But the same warning also covers the dtype-mismatch cases above, where nothing is absent. When it is enforced, `pd.Series([1, 2]).astype(pd.CategoricalDtype(pd.Index(["1", "2"])))` will raise, with a message pointing at the wrong cause.

### Scope

Sweeping 10 value dtypes × 5 category dtypes (50 combos) on `3.1.0.dev0+1520.gebd40365c94`, comparing one-step `astype(CategoricalDtype(cats))` against two-step `astype(cats.dtype)` + `Categorical(...)`:

- **25** agree.
- **11** where the two-step cast succeeds and the one-step is silently all-NaN. Includes `object`/`str` values of `"1"`, `"2"` against `int64`/`Int64`/`float64` categories; `int64`/`Int64`/`int64[pyarrow]` values against `str` categories; `ArrowDtype(pa.string())` values against `M8[s]` categories.
- **14** where the two-step cast raises and the one-step is silently all-NaN, e.g. non-numeric strings against `int64` categories. Here the lookup is merely laxer than a cast.

### Proposal

Cast to `dtype.categories.dtype` first, then look up. Group 2 then round-trips correctly, and group 3 raises a genuine cast error instead of a "not in categories" message that misidentifies the cause. Group 1 is unaffected.

The alternative is to keep lookup semantics and accept that legitimate casts raise once GH-62142 is enforced, which seems hard to justify to users.

Related: GH-62051 is one instance of this (`ArrowDtype` string values against timedelta/datetime categories), which is what surfaced it.

title: BUG: concat with null[pyarrow] altered the other columns' dtype (GH#62343)
body:
closes #62343

`ArrowDtype._get_common_dtype` drops `null[pyarrow]` from the input list but still round-trips every remaining dtype through `numpy_dtype` and re-wraps with `pa.from_numpy_dtype`. That round-trip is lossy for pyarrow types with no numpy analogue, so mixing any of them with `null[pyarrow]` corrupted the result:

| dtype combined with `null[pyarrow]` | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `date32` / `date64` | `timestamp[ms]` | preserved |
| `timestamp[us, tz=US/Pacific]` | `timestamp[us]` — tz dropped, values converted to UTC | preserved |
| `time32` / `time64` / `decimal128` / `binary` / `list<...>` | `object` | preserved |
| `large_string` | `string` | preserved |

Fixed by short-circuiting before the numpy round-trip when the non-null dtypes are all a single `ArrowDtype` — null promotes to anything, so there is nothing to resolve.

This is not concat-specific: `.loc` setitem-with-expansion on a `date32` index hit the same path, since an NA label enters as `null[pyarrow]`. Two xfail overrides in `test_arrow.py` are now obsolete and removed — `test_get_common_dtype` (which xfailed precisely the date/time/tz-timestamp/binary/decimal set) and `test_loc_setitem_with_expansion_preserves_ea_index_dtype`.

Not addressed here: `large_string` + `string` still gives `string`, and `null[pyarrow]` + `Int64` still gives `object`. Switching wholesale to pyarrow's own promotion (`pa.unify_schemas(..., promote_options="permissive")`) would cover those, but it diverges from pandas semantics elsewhere — pyarrow gives `int64` for `int8` + `uint64` where pandas gives `float64`, and raises on `bool` + `int64`.

title: BUG: read_csv parallel path takes the corrupting path for falsy non-False low_memory (GH#66259)
body:
The `low_memory` gate in `_can_parallelize_csv` added by GH-66327 (addressing Bug 3 of GH-66259) tested identity:

```python
if kwds.get("low_memory") is False:
    return False
```

But `low_memory` is never coerced to `bool`, and the serial path branches on truthiness (`if self.low_memory:` in `CParserWrapper.read`). So `low_memory=0` and `np.False_` promised whole-file type inference to the serial reader while slipping past the parallel guard — reintroducing exactly the silent corruption that gate exists to prevent.

Verified on a 6MB uint64-conflict CSV (200k `hello` rows, then alternating `nan` / `9223372036854775808`) with `mode.max_threads=4`:

| `low_memory` | NA count | literal `"nan"` |
|---|---|---|
| `False` | 200000 | 0 |
| `0` | **12501** | **187499** |
| `np.False_` | **12501** | **187499** |

Silent — no exception, no warning. All three agree at `max_threads=1`. Both columns are `str` dtype, so the gather's per-column dtype reconciliation cannot see the divergence.

The fix tests truthiness instead, defaulting to `True` to match `_c_parser_defaults`, so an unset `low_memory` stays eligible for the parallel path:

```python
if not kwds.get("low_memory", True):
    return False
```

Tests: parametrized the two existing `low_memory` tests over `[False, 0, np.False_]` — the `_can_parallelize_csv` guard check and the end-to-end uint64-conflict serial-comparison test. Reverting the one-line fix fails all four new cases and passes the two `False` ones.

No whatsnew entry: parallel `read_csv` is itself new in unreleased 3.1.0, so this never shipped.

Note on GH-66259: deliberately no closing keyword. That issue bundles six divergences and several are still live — Bug 1 (`EmptyDataError` on a headerless file with a leading blank line, open PR GH-66344), Bug 5 (per-chunk duplicated `ParserWarning`), Bug 6 (deferred mmap unmap on the error path). This PR only closes the leak in the Bug 3 gate. No overlap with GH-66344, which touches `readers.py` elsewhere.

title: PERF: vectorize datetimelike array addition when the bounds allow it (GH#66552)
body:
Addresses the "Performance" section of GH-66552.

`add_overflowsafe` backs add/subtract for `DatetimeArray`, `TimedeltaArray` and `PeriodArray`, and so for the corresponding Index and Series. It loops per element to check both for int64 overflow and for a result landing on the `NaT` sentinel, which costs about 12x a plain numpy add.

Take min/max of both operands first. If the bounds prove every sum stays inside `(iNaT, INT64_MAX]`, then no element can overflow or land on the sentinel, and the addition can go to numpy in one vectorized pass. The bounds are conservative in the safe direction — a batch that could overflow falls back to the loop — so no result can skip a guard. This is the same shape as the existing fast path in `astype_overflowsafe` a few hundred lines up, which the issue points at as the model.

The two reductions cost a fixed ~1us that the loop does not pay, putting the crossover at a few hundred elements, so small inputs stay on the loop rather than regressing.

1M elements, macOS arm64:

| | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `DatetimeIndex + Timedelta` | 5.04 ms | 0.41 ms |
| `DatetimeIndex - DatetimeIndex` | 6.91 ms | 1.31 ms |
| `TimedeltaIndex + Timedelta` | 4.41 ms | 0.39 ms |
| `PeriodIndex + 1` | 6.14 ms | 0.40 ms |
| `DatetimeIndex + Day(1)` | 6.13 ms | 0.43 ms |

`add_overflowsafe` had no direct tests, and no existing test used an array large enough to reach the new path, so the added tests are parametrized over a size on each side of the threshold. I checked they are not vacuous by mutating each bound to be one off; both mutations fail, and only at the large size.

title: BUG: Period minus Period raised OverflowError for a count of INT64_MIN (GH#66552)

labels.name: Missing-data
labels.description: np.nan, pd.NaT, pd.NA, dropna, isnull, interpolate

body:
Addresses the "Where `INT64_MIN` is legitimate" item of GH-66552.

`add_overflowsafe` rejects a sum landing exactly on `NPY_NAT`, since as a datetime64 or timedelta64 value it would be indistinguishable from a missing one. That guard landed in GH-66602 without the opt-out GH-66552 calls for, so `Period` minus `Period` — which returns a *count* of periods rather than an ordinal — started raising for a result the scalar path still gives:

```python
>>> left = pd.PeriodIndex([pd.Period(ordinal=-(2**62), freq="D")])
>>> right = pd.PeriodIndex([pd.Period(ordinal=2**62, freq="D")])

>>> left[0] - right[0]        # scalar, correct
<-9223372036854775808 * Days>

>>> left - right              # on main
OverflowError: Overflow in int64 addition
```

Gate the result check behind a `sentinel_ok` flag and pass it from `_sub_periodlike`, the one caller whose result is a count. NaT operands still short-circuit to NaT, and genuine int64 overflow still raises.

`_sub_periodlike` now also builds its offsets from python ints rather than iterating the int64 array directly. Feeding a `np.int64` of `INT64_MIN` to `BaseOffset.__mul__` trips a spurious `RuntimeWarning: overflow encountered in scalar multiply` on Windows, where numpy's scalar-multiply overflow check falls back off `__builtin_mul_overflow` and misfires on `INT64_MIN`. The `ravel()`/`reshape()` is load-bearing: `PeriodArray` can be 2D, and `tolist()` on a 2D array would hand `__mul__` nested lists.

No whatsnew: the regression was introduced and fixed within the unreleased 3.1.0 dev cycle, and the existing entry describes the ordinal-producing paths, which are unaffected.

As GH-66552 notes, nothing covered this — a full `pandas/tests` run passes with `PeriodArray - PeriodArray` regressed — so the tests here pin down both the count (array/Index/Series, against the scalar) and that the opt-out does not leak: a genuine `2**63` overflow still raises, an ordinal landing on the sentinel still raises, and NaT operands still propagate.

title: BUG: unstack(sort=False) placed values under wrong row labels (GH#62816)
body:
closes #62816

`_Unstacker` numbered the result rows in two different ways, and the two only agreed when at most one level was left after the unstack. Values were placed in row `comp_index`, which `get_compressed_ids` numbers lexicographically by the remaining levels' codes, while the row labels came from `compressor`, which numbered them by first appearance. With `sort=False` those orders diverge, so values landed under the wrong labels — silently, with no error or warning.

The issue's own example:

```python
df.value_counts(subset=["Department", "Gender", "Location"]).unstack(fill_value=0, sort=False)
```

Two further shapes of the same defect, both fixed here:

* One remaining level is enough once the unstacked level contains NaN — a different mechanism (the sort indexer rather than the `compressor`/`comp_index` disagreement).
* With two or more remaining levels it could do worse than mislabel: distinct index combinations were collapsed into a single row, dropping data.

The fix compresses the remaining levels once, with `sort=self.sort`, so the group number *is* the row's position in the result; the sort indexer and `compressor` are then derived from that single numbering. `new_index` no longer needs a `sort` branch.

`sort=True` behaviour is unchanged — the indexer, ngroups, result codes and selector set are identical to before over a large randomized comparison — and `sort=False` gets faster (~1.75x on 400k rows), since the old code re-factorized every level separately; the rewrite also drops the `sorted_labels` materialization.

The `sort` docstrings for both methods said the flag only sorts the resulting MultiIndex columns; it also determines the row order, which is what this PR is about, so they are corrected too.

Two neighbouring `unstack(sort=False)` label bugs turned up while testing this. Both are independent of the numbering fix and are left for follow-ups: GH-66672 (`Series.unstack` puts the NaN column first while its values stay in place) and GH-66673 (columns mislabelled when the unstacked level has unused entries).

title: BUG: Day offset added to a tz-aware DatetimeIndex wrapped or landed on the NaT sentinel (GH#66552)
body:
Part of GH-66552 (the `Day._apply_array` entry in its inventory).

`Day._apply_array` added with a raw numpy add. It is reached only for tz-aware data — tz-naive `Day` addition is routed through `_add_timedeltalike_scalar`, which already goes via `add_overflowsafe` — so the two disagreed:

```python
dti = pd.DatetimeIndex([pd.Timestamp(iNaT + 86400 * 10**9)])

dti + pd.offsets.Day(-1)                      # OverflowError
dti.tz_localize("UTC") + pd.offsets.Day(-1)   # NaT           <- silently missing
dti.tz_localize("UTC") + pd.offsets.Day(-2)   # 2262-04-10    <- silently wrapped
```

This mirrors `Week._apply_array`: convert `n` to the array's own unit with `checked_mul`, reject a shift that is itself the sentinel, then add through `add_overflowsafe`. That also closes a third hole the raw add had — an `n` large enough to overflow int64 during the unit conversion.

In-bounds results and `NaT` propagation are unchanged.

title: BUG: rolling cov/corr wrong after a large value leaves the window (GH#65739)
body:
Follow-up to GH-65739, which replaced the `mean(xy) - mean(x)mean(y)` implementation of `Rolling.cov`/`Rolling.corr` with an incremental one. Two ways the new code returns wrong results, both found while differential-testing against exact rational arithmetic. No released version is affected.

### Cancellation was only detected in `ssqdm_xy`, and only one update deep

`ssqdm_x`/`ssqdm_y` collapse to `eps * peak_dev ** 2` of round-off as soon as the value that dominated them leaves the window — that is the sensitive signal, and it was not tested at all. The `ssqdm_xy` test compared against its own value one update earlier, so error introduced by an *earlier* removal was already invisible. Every window after a large value left was silently wrong, or `NaN` once a negative `ssqdm_x` reached the square root in `calc_corr`:

```python
x = pd.Series([1.0, 2.0, 1e12, 1e7, 6.0, 5.0, 8.0, 7.0])
y = pd.Series([2.0, 1.0, 3.0, -1e12, 4.0, 7.0, 6.0, 9.0])

x.rolling(3).corr(y).iloc[-1]   # nan      exact: -0.14285714285714285
x.rolling(3).cov(y).iloc[-1]    # -5.9e+07 exact: -0.3333333333333333
```

The error is now bounded by the largest deviation each accumulator has absorbed since the last recompute, and all three accumulators are tested against that bound. `roll_cov` accumulates `ssqdm_x`/`ssqdm_y` purely to feed the test; `calc_cov` never reads them.

### Deviations were taken against a mean that is itself huge

With an offset shared by the whole series — prices, epoch timestamps — almost no significant digits survive, and no outlier is needed anywhere in the data:

```python
x = pd.Series([1, 2, 4, 7, 3, 5, 9, 2, 6, 8], dtype="float64") + 1e12
y = pd.Series([2, 1, 5, 3, 8, 4, 7, 9, 1, 6], dtype="float64") + 1e12

x.rolling(5).cov(y).iloc[4:7].tolist()
# [1.099968..., -0.300072..., -0.800026...]   exact: [1.1, -0.3, -0.8]
```

The accumulators are now anchored to the first value in the window, so a shared offset cancels exactly rather than costing precision in every deviation. A value large enough that `val - origin` could overflow is not used as an anchor, which keeps a window spanning most of the float64 range from poisoning the accumulators with `NaN`.

### Verification

Across ~150k windows checked against `fractions.Fraction`, no window now exceeds 1e-3 relative error — the `InvCondTol` tolerance this module is designed to hold to. On the same corpus `main` has 550 such windows for `cov` and 3090 (plus 1382 spurious `NaN`) for `corr`. Both are now at least as accurate as the pre-GH-65739 implementation on every case I could construct, including the large-offset shapes that one handled badly, and recompute frequency and wall clock are unchanged.

title: BUG: setitem-with-expansion saturating or raising for integer EA dtypes (GH#65094)

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

labels.name: ExtensionArray
labels.description: Extending pandas with custom dtypes or arrays.

labels.name: NA - MaskedArrays
labels.description: Related to pd.NA and nullable extension arrays

body:
Follow-up to GH-65094, which added an integer-ExtensionArray branch to `infer_and_maybe_downcast`. That branch verified a float->int cast by roundtripping the result back through the ExtensionArray, which has two problems:

- The roundtrip is blind to saturation, since e.g. `2**63` and `int64max` are the same `float64`. `Series([1, 2], dtype="Int64").loc[2] = 2.0**63` silently stored `int64max` and kept `Int64`. Same for `UInt64` + `2.0**64` and for `Sparse[int64]`.
- For `ArrowDtype` the reverse leg raises: pyarrow refuses its own `int64->double` cast above `2**53`. `Series([1, 2], dtype="int64[pyarrow]").loc[2] = 1.7e18` raised `pyarrow.lib.ArrowInvalid` out of `.loc`, even though the value converts exactly.

Both now go through `floats_fit_integer_dtype` (the helper the numpy path already uses, from GH-66394), and the truncation check is done in numpy float space instead of roundtripping through the EA. The three backends agree afterwards:

| value into | `int64` (numpy) | `Int64` | `int64[pyarrow]` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `1.7e18` | `int64` | `Int64` | `int64[pyarrow]` (was `ArrowInvalid`) |
| `2.0**63` | `float64` | `Float64` (was silently `int64max`) | `double[pyarrow]` (was `ArrowInvalid`) |

No whatsnew entry: GH-65094 has not appeared in a release, so this is dev-only.

title: BUG: loc/iloc setitem transposing nested values on single-block frames (GH#65241)

labels.name: Indexing
labels.description: Related to indexing on series/frames, not to indexes themselves

body:
GH-65241 fixed GH-44103 (`df.loc[0, ["a"]] = ["one"]` raising on a single-column ExtensionArray frame) by forcing the split path for a scalar row plus list-like columns on any single-block frame. But the non-split path only mishandles list-like values on ExtensionArray blocks; on ndarray blocks the split path reads a rectangular nested value as rows x columns, so on an object-dtype frame:

```python
df = DataFrame({"a": [1, "x"], "b": [2, "y"]}, dtype=object)
df.loc[0, ["a", "b"]] = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
# a=[1, 3], b=[2, 4]  -- transposed; was a=[1, 2], b=[3, 4]
```

A list of tuples was transposed and retyped to lists, and single-column (`[[1, 2]]`) or ragged (`[[1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]`) values raised `ValueError`.

Gate the branch on `Block.is_extension` so it applies only where the GH-44103 bug actually occurs. Since EA blocks are 1D, that is the single-column EA case the original fix targeted. Note `is_extension` is narrower than "not an ndarray": `datetime64`/`timedelta64` blocks hold a `DatetimeArray`/`TimedeltaArray` but are not extension blocks, and the non-split path handles them correctly.

No whatsnew entry: GH-65241 landed in the unreleased 3.1.0, so the regression never shipped.

The tests parametrize over `loc`/`iloc` and over list, boolean-mask, and slice column keys, since the gate's `not is_integer(indexer[1])` clause admits all of them.

title: BUG: DataFrame.unstack(sort=False) mislabels columns when the unstacked level has unused entries
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

# "y" is present in the level but used by no row
mi = pd.MultiIndex(
    levels=[["a", "b"], ["x", "y", "z"]],
    codes=[[0, 0, 1, 1], [2, 0, 2, 0]],
    names=["r", "c"],
)
df = pd.DataFrame({"v": [1.0, 2, 3, 4]}, index=mi)

print(df.unstack(sort=False))          # wrong labels
print(df["v"].unstack(sort=False))     # correct
print(df["v"].astype("Int64").unstack(sort=False).columns.tolist())  # wrong
```

### Issue Description

When the unstacked level contains an entry that no row uses, `DataFrame.unstack(sort=False)`
labels the result columns with the wrong level entries. The values are placed correctly, so the
data is silently mislabelled:

```
     v
c    x    y      <- wrong; should be z, x
r
a  1.0  2.0
b  3.0  4.0
```

`Series.unstack` on the same data gives the correct `z, x`, so the two disagree. An
extension-dtype `Series` is *also* wrong, because it routes through `_unstack_extension_series`
-> `DataFrame.unstack` (last line above prints `['x', 'y']`).

Cause: `_Unstacker.__init__` sets `self.removed_level_full = index.levels[self.level]` from the
index *before* `remove_unused_levels()`, then in the `sort=False` branch takes it with
`unique_codes`, which index the level *after* removal:

```python
self.removed_level = self.removed_level.take(unique_codes)
self.removed_level_full = self.removed_level_full.take(unique_codes)   # wrong basis
```

Because that take always leaves `len(removed_level_full) == len(removed_level)`, `_repeater`
then takes its `arange` branch and never remaps, so the bad labels reach
`get_new_columns` unchecked. With a `NaN` in the level too
(`codes=[[0,0,1,1],[2,-1,2,0]]`) the result is `x, nan, y` instead of `z, nan, x`.

This only bites when `remove_unused_levels()` actually drops something; otherwise the pre- and
post-removal levels are identical and the take is harmless.

### Expected Behavior

`df.unstack(sort=False)` should label the columns `z, x`, matching the values and matching
`Series.unstack`.

### Installed Versions

<details>

Reproduced on main at `ff1d39bbdf4` (`3.1.0.dev0+1512.gff1d39bbdf4`). Also present in 2.x.

</details>

title: BUG: Series.unstack(sort=False) puts the NaN column first while its values stay in place
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

ser = pd.Series(
    [1.0, 2.0, 3.0],
    index=pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples(
        [("r", 8.0), ("r", 7.0), ("r", np.nan)], names=["x", "z"]
    ),
)
print(ser.unstack(1, sort=False))
print(ser.to_frame("v").unstack(1, sort=False))
```

### Issue Description

With `sort=False`, `Series.unstack` places the `NaN` column of the unstacked level at position 0,
but the *values* stay at the position where `NaN` first appeared. Every column ends up mislabelled:

```
z  NaN  8.0  7.0
x
r  1.0  2.0  3.0
```

`1.0` belongs to `8.0`, `2.0` to `7.0` and `3.0` to `NaN`, so each value is shifted one column left.
Nothing raises and nothing warns.

`DataFrame.unstack` on the same data is correct, so the two paths disagree:

```
     v
z  8.0  7.0  NaN
x
r  1.0  2.0  3.0
```

The divergence is in `_Unstacker.get_new_columns`: the `value_columns is None` branch (used by
`Series.unstack` with a numpy dtype) does `self.removed_level.insert(0, ...)` unconditionally,
while the `value_columns is not None` branch derives the position from `self._repeater`, which
honours `self.unique_nan_index`. Only the `sort=True` case wants position 0 (that is what
`self.lift` does); with `sort=False` the values are never lifted.

Note an extension-dtype `Series` routes through `_unstack_extension_series` -> `DataFrame.unstack`,
so it takes the correct branch — only the numpy-dtype `Series` path is affected.

### Expected Behavior

`ser.unstack(1, sort=False)` should give columns `[8.0, 7.0, NaN]`, matching the values and matching
`DataFrame.unstack`.

### Installed Versions

<details>

Reproduced on main at `ff1d39bbdf4` (`3.1.0.dev0+1512.gff1d39bbdf4`). Also present in 2.x.

</details>

title: BUG: to_datetime/to_timedelta with narrow NumPy scalars and a unit (GH#56996)

labels.name: Compat
labels.description: pandas objects compatability with Numpy or Python functions

body:
closes #56996

`cast_from_unit` splits its input into an integer `base` and a fractional part, then multiplies each by the unit factor `m`. The fractional part kept the input's own NumPy dtype, so under NEP 50 that multiply happened at the narrow width:

```python
>>> pd.to_timedelta([np.int8(1)], unit="D")      # np.int8(0) * 86400 -> OverflowError
OutOfBoundsTimedelta: Cannot cast 1 from D to 's' without overflow.
>>> pd.to_timedelta([np.int8(1)], unit="D", errors="coerce")
TimedeltaIndex([NaT], dtype='timedelta64[s]')

>>> pd.Timedelta(np.float32(1.5), "D")
Timedelta('1 days 12:00:00.001605632')
>>> pd.Timedelta(np.float16(1.5), "D")           # round(x, 13) overflows to NaN
ValueError: cannot convert float NaN to integer
```

Widening to a Python int/float at the top of `cast_from_unit` makes the arithmetic match the builtin-scalar case. GH-63302 previously routed integer *scalars* around this via `np.timedelta64`, so the scalar constructors already worked for ints — the object/list path and all float input did not.

This also fixes `unit="Y"`/`unit="M"` for *every* NumPy integer, `np.int64` included, since numpy rejects any NumPy integer scalar in `np.datetime64(x, "Y")`:

```python
>>> pd.to_datetime([np.int64(150)], unit="Y")
ValueError: Could not convert object to NumPy datetime
```

Three sentinel comparisons had a related NEP 50 hazard: testing a raw NumPy float against the int64 `NPY_NAT` cast the sentinel down to the narrow dtype. For `np.float16` that emitted a spurious `RuntimeWarning: overflow encountered in cast` (an error under the test suite's `filterwarnings`), and since `-2**63` saturates to `-inf` in float16, `np.float16("-inf")` compared equal to the sentinel and silently became `NaT` while the wider float dtypes correctly raised.

The vectorized path is unaffected — both callers of `cast_from_unit_vectorized` already `.astype("float64")` first.

Note: with NumPy integers now taking the same path Python integers always took, `to_datetime([np.uint64(2**63 + 5)], unit="Y")` raises a bare `OverflowError` rather than the previous `ValueError`. That pre-existing gap (Python ints already behaved this way, and round floats still do for every unit) is GH-60677 and is left for a follow-up.

title: BUG: Timedelta divided by a float array saturated (GH#66552)
body:
Part of GH-66552 — the division half of its "`Timedelta` `+`/`-`/`*`/`/` with an ndarray" item. The add/subtract half landed in GH-66661 and the multiplication half in GH-66668.

`Timedelta.__truediv__` and `__floordiv__` hand a float ndarray straight to numpy, which saturates a quotient that leaves the `int64` range instead of reporting it. `TimedeltaIndex` already raises:

```python
>>> Timedelta(4, "ns") / np.array([1e-300])
array([9223372036854775807], dtype='timedelta64[ns]')
>>> pd.TimedeltaIndex([Timedelta(4, "ns")]) / np.array([1e-300])
OutOfBoundsTimedelta: Overflow in timedelta division
```

Both `/` and `//` now raise `OutOfBoundsTimedelta`, reusing the message the `TimedeltaIndex` path already uses. Zero and nan divisors still come back as `NaT` — numpy calls those missing rather than out of bounds, and so does the array path. Integer divisors need no check: a quotient can only exceed the dividend when the divisor lies between -1 and 1.

Not fixed here, still open on GH-66552: the tz-aware `DatetimeArray._add_offset` fast path (a tz-aware `DatetimeIndex + Day(-1)` landing on the sentinel still returns `NaT` where the naive one raises) and `Week._end_apply_index` (a weekday-anchored `Week` still wraps).

title: BUG: Timedelta multiplied by a numeric array wrapped or saturated (GH#66552)
body:
Part of GH-66552 (one of the remaining sentinel/overflow gaps; the issue stays open for the rest).

`Timedelta.__mul__` / `__rmul__` with an integer- or float-dtype ndarray deferred straight to numpy, so an out-of-bounds product silently wrapped or saturated, and one landing exactly on `int64.min` came back as `NaT`. The `TimedeltaIndex` equivalent already raises `OutOfBoundsTimedelta` for all of these (GH-43178), so this was a scalar/array disagreement with the silently-wrong answer on the scalar side:

```python
>>> pd.Timedelta(4, "ns") * np.array([2**62])
array([0], dtype='timedelta64[ns]')                    # wrapped
>>> pd.Timedelta(4, "ns") * np.array([-(2**63)])
array([0], dtype='timedelta64[ns]')
>>> pd.Timedelta(4, "ns") * np.array([1e30])
array([9223372036854775807], dtype='timedelta64[ns]')  # saturated
>>> pd.Timedelta(4, "ns") * np.array([np.inf])
array(['NaT'], dtype='timedelta64[ns]')
>>> pd.Timedelta(4, "ns") * np.array([2**63], dtype=np.uint64)
array([0], dtype='timedelta64[ns]')
```

All five now raise `OutOfBoundsTimedelta`, matching `TimedeltaIndex` element for element.

For the integer path the two extreme multipliers bound every product, so checking those with exact Python-int arithmetic lets the common no-overflow case use a plain vectorized multiply; the bound excludes `int64.min` itself, which is representable but would be misread as `NaT`. The float path forms the product in float64 and compares against `2**63` rather than `int64.max` (which rounds up to `2**63` in float64, so a product landing there would slip past and saturate on the cast). A `NaN` multiplier still gives `NaT` — that is a missing value, not an overflow — and bool, object and `timedelta64` operands keep deferring to numpy unchanged.

Widening to float64 also fixes a precision gap in the same path: numpy kept a `float32` multiplier's product in float32, so `Timedelta(10**18, "ns") * np.array([1.0], dtype="f4")` returned `999999984306749440ns` where `TimedeltaIndex` returned the exact value.

Cost is 1.15x a raw numpy multiply at 1M elements for integers and 2.2x for floats, the same profile as `TimedeltaArray`'s existing overflow-safe multiply.

title: BUG: read_hdf returned a sentinel string for missing values appended to a MultiIndex level in an older file (GH#9604)

labels.name: Missing-data
labels.description: np.nan, pd.NaT, pd.NA, dropna, isnull, interpolate

body:
Follow-up to GH-66330 (GH-9604), which gave each string `MultiIndex` level its own NaN sentinel so a literal `"nan"` and a genuine missing value could both round-trip.

The writer mints that sentinel unconditionally, but the reader honors it only when the table carries the `mi_level_nan_rep` marker attribute. `set_attrs` writes the marker when the table is created and an append cannot add it retroactively, so appending a missing value to a `MultiIndex` file written by an older pandas stored the sentinel while the reader still used the global `nan_rep`:

```python
# level already holding "nan", in a file written before the marker existed
mi1 = MultiIndex.from_arrays([Index(["nan", "wide_value"], dtype=str), [1, 2]])
Series(range(2), index=mi1).to_hdf(path, key="t", format="table", append=True)

mi2 = MultiIndex.from_arrays([Index([np.nan, "y"], dtype=str), [3, 4]])
Series(range(2, 4), index=mi2).to_hdf(path, key="t", format="table", append=True)

list(read_hdf(path, "t").index.get_level_values(0))
# [nan, 'wide_value', '_nan_', 'y']   <- the appended missing value
```

The appended `NaN` came back as the literal string `'_nan_'`, silently and with no warning.

Appending to a table without the marker now keeps encoding missing values with the global `nan_rep`, which is what the reader applies to such a file — restoring the pre-GH-66330 behavior for it exactly. Files created since GH-66330 carry the marker and keep the full per-level round-trip.

The plain string `Index` path is unaffected: its sentinel is read back unconditionally from the per-column attribute, and a missing value in a legacy file already read back as the string `"nan"` both before and after an append, so minting a sentinel there does not reinterpret existing rows.

No whatsnew entry — GH-66330 is unreleased, so the existing 3.1.0 note still describes the shipped behavior.

title: DEPR: select_dtypes non-standard datetimetz/period dtype strings (GH#24558)
body:
closes #24558

`DataFrame.select_dtypes` accepts two made-up dtype strings, `"datetimetz"` and `"datetime64tz"`, and raises a bare message-less `NotImplementedError` for `"period"`. Both are now handled in favor of the dtype classes, which already select the corresponding dtype families as of GH-65366:

- `"datetimetz"` / `"datetime64tz"` emit a `Pandas4Warning` recommending `pd.DatetimeTZDtype`. They still select the same columns.
- `"period"` raises a `TypeError` pointing at `pd.PeriodDtype` (all period columns) or a string such as `"period[D]"` (one frequency). Since it never worked, there is no behavior to deprecate — only an error message worth making useful. `TypeError` also matches what every other unsupported string already raises via `pandas_dtype`.

The tz strings now resolve to the `DatetimeTZDtype` class rather than `DatetimeTZDtype.type`. This selects the same columns, but makes them genuinely interchangeable with the replacement the warning recommends: previously `include="datetimetz", exclude=pd.DatetimeTZDtype` resolved to two different specs, so the overlap check missed it and the call silently returned an empty frame instead of raising.

The plotting internals were the only in-tree callers of the deprecated string — `DataFrame.plot` and `DataFrame.hist` picked their plottable columns with `"datetimetz"`, which made the new warning fire from inside pandas on ordinary plotting calls. They now pass `DatetimeTZDtype`, selecting the same columns.

title: BUG: Timedelta added to a timedelta64 array wrapped or landed on NaT (GH#66552)

labels.name: Missing-data
labels.description: np.nan, pd.NaT, pd.NA, dropna, isnull, interpolate

body:
One code path from the GH-66552 inventory: `Timedelta` +/- a `timedelta64` ndarray. The issue is not closed by this — it covers many more sites.

`Timedelta.__add__`/`__radd__`/`__sub__`/`__rsub__` handed the whole operation to numpy for an `m8` ndarray operand, so all three failure modes from the issue were live at once:

```python
>>> Timedelta.min + np.array([-1], "m8[ns]")
array(["NaT"], dtype="timedelta64[ns]")      # sum fits in int64 but *is* iNaT
>>> Timedelta.min + np.array([-2], "m8[ns]")
array([9223372036854775807], dtype="timedelta64[ns]")   # wrapped past int64
>>> Timedelta(10**12, "s") + np.array([1], "m8[ns]")
array([3875820019684212737], dtype="timedelta64[ns]")   # wrapped on the s -> ns promotion
```

Each of these already raised for the equivalent scalar and `TimedeltaIndex` operations. They now raise `OutOfBoundsTimedelta`, anchored to the scalar `Timedelta` neighbour rather than to the index one, since the operands here are a scalar and a raw ndarray.

All four dunders go through one new `_addsub_timedelta64_array` helper in `timedeltas.pyx`, deliberately the mirror of the same-named helper added to `timestamps.pyx` in GH-66581 for the reversed operand order. `NaT` inputs still propagate as missing; `__sub__` negates the array (`NPY_NAT` negates to itself) while `__rsub__` negates the scalar, which is never `NaT`.

Year/month and sub-nanosecond units are left to numpy — it refuses the former itself, and we have no reso for the latter. Verified the result is byte-identical to the plain numpy add across a 4 x 8 x 4 matrix of Timedelta unit x array unit x operator, plus generic `m8`, byte-swapped, 2D, non-contiguous and empty input.

Deliberately left alone, still wrapping:

- the `M` branch of the same `elif` (`Timedelta` + a `datetime64` ndarray, e.g. `Timedelta(1, "ns") + np.array(["2500-01-01"], "M8[s]")` -> 1915) — a datetime64 result with a different exception family
- `Timedelta` `*` and `/` with an ndarray, which GH-66552 files under "adjacent, not sentinel-specific" with an open question about which exception to match

One tradeoff worth flagging: this path was previously a bare numpy add, so it now pays the `add_overflowsafe` cost — about 5x on 1M elements (1.28 ms -> 6.05 ms). That is the same cost the other array paths in this series already pay, and the min/max fast path proposed in the Performance section of GH-66552 would recover it for every caller at once. Happy to add a local pre-check here instead if that is preferred.

title: BUG: read_csv crashed instead of raising when an allocation failed mid-error
body:
The C parser built every error message with `malloc()` + `snprintf()` and never checked the allocation:

```c
self->error_msg = (char *)malloc(bufsize);
snprintf(self->error_msg, bufsize, "Buffer overflow caught ...");
```

If that `malloc` fails, `snprintf` is handed a NULL destination — undefined behaviour, and in practice a segfault instead of the `ParserError` the caller expects. There were 10 such sites. Two related leaks came along for the ride: overwriting an existing `error_msg` dropped the old one, and `parser_trim_buffers` assigned `realloc`'s result straight back to `word_ends`, leaking the old buffer and storing NULL if a shrink ever failed.

Rather than add a NULL check at each site, this removes the allocation. Every message is a constant or a short format over a few integers, so they now live in a fixed buffer inside `parser_t`; `error_msg` points into it and is never freed. Nothing is allocated on an error path, so nothing there can fail. Warnings format into a separate `warn_buf` so building one can never rewrite a pending error message out from under `error_msg`. `warn_msg` genuinely accumulates across bad lines, so it stays heap-allocated and is now NULL-checked.

Error and warning text is unchanged, including multi-warning accumulation.

## Performance

Deleting the inline `malloc`/`snprintf` blocks shrinks `_tokenize_helper` (where `tokenize_bytes` inlines) from 7276 to 7012 bytes, and the hot loop gets slightly denser. Full 123-case read_csv suite, adaptive 8-40 rounds to a ±0.75% CI target, 99% intervals with a 1% effect floor, against a pinned baseline:

| | median | worst | regressions | improvements |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| this PR | 1.0104 | 0.9958 | **0** | 63 |
| null control (identical binary) | 1.0002 | 0.9923 | 0 | 0 |
| layout control (identical semantics, code shifted) | 1.0005 | 0.9918 | 0 | 6 |

No case regresses; the worst case anywhere is 0.9958, below the effect floor and inside the layout control's own envelope. The speedup is incidental — the point of the PR is the crash — but it is comfortably outside what code-placement noise produces.

One implementation note worth preserving: `parser_append_warningf` must stay a function call. `end_line` runs once per row, and inlining the varargs format into it measured ~5% slower on the quoted and escaped-quote cases. There is a comment on it saying so.

title: fix stream buffer overflow in read_csv c engine on short rows
body:
1. read_csv with the ``c`` engine reserves the token stream once per read buffer for a 1:1 copy of the input, and the SIMD/scalar bulk-copy fast paths in ``tokenize_bytes`` then write field bytes with no per-copy capacity check.
2. a row with fewer fields than expected is padded in ``end_line`` with one synthetic NUL terminator per missing field; those writes take stream space but consume no input, and only ``make_stream_space(ex_fields - fields)`` was reserved for them, not the input still waiting to be copied.
3. a read buffer with many short rows before a wide field then leaves the stream smaller than that field, so the bulk copy runs past ``self->stream`` (heap-buffer-overflow under ASAN; without a sanitizer the field is truncated or corrupted, and larger inputs crash).

Reserve room for the terminators plus the rest of the chunk so the reservation the bulk copies rely on survives the padding.

title: BUG: read_csv (c engine) heap buffer overflow on short rows before a wide field
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import io
import pandas as pd

n_cols = 5000
wide = "X" * 100_000
# many rows shorter than n_cols, then one wide field, all in one read buffer
data = "a\n" * 40 + wide + "\n"

df = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(data), header=None, names=[f"c{i}" for i in range(n_cols)])
print(df.shape)                 # (41, 5000) as expected
print(len(df.iloc[40, 0]))      # 99999, but the field is 100000 chars
```

### Issue Description

With the C engine, `read_csv` reserves the token stream once per read buffer for the
worst case that the whole buffer is copied 1:1, and the SIMD/scalar bulk-copy fast paths
in `tokenize_bytes` then write field bytes with no per-copy capacity check. When a row has
fewer fields than expected, `end_line` closes the missing fields by writing a NUL
terminator for each one. Those synthetic terminators take stream space but consume no
input, so a run of short rows eats into the reservation the bulk copies rely on. It is
restored only for the terminators themselves (`make_stream_space(ex_fields - fields)`),
not for the input still waiting to be copied.

So a buffer that holds many short rows followed by a wide field ends up with the stream
smaller than that field, and the bulk copy runs past the end of `self->stream`. Building
with ASAN (`-Db_sanitize=address`) reports a `heap-buffer-overflow` WRITE at the
`memcpy`/`*stream++` in `tokenize_bytes`; without a sanitizer the field is silently
truncated or corrupted as above, and larger inputs crash the interpreter. `names=` is one
easy way in because it makes every data row subject to the short-row padding, but any
source with short rows before a wide field in the same 256 KiB read chunk reaches it.

The bulk-copy paths and the reservation live in
`pandas/_libs/src/parser/tokenizer.cpp` (`tokenize_bytes`, `end_line`).

### Expected Behavior

The frame parses without reading or writing past the stream buffer, and the wide field
comes back intact (`len(df.iloc[40, 0]) == 100000`).

<details>

Reproduced on the current main branch (commit e0839ed).

</details>

few lines. Every code example and behavioral claim below was run against

user guide pages build clean.

**Docs that were factually wrong**

- `display.date_dayfirst` / `date_yearfirst` said they "print and parse"
  dates. They only affect parsing, and only in `Period` construction and
  partial-string `DatetimeIndex` indexing — the two `get_option` calls in
  `parsing.pyx` are the only consumers, and `Timestamp` / `to_datetime` /
  `read_csv` take their own keyword.
- `DatetimeIndex.to_period` / `DatetimeArray.to_period` documented
  `freq : str or Period`, but a `Period` is rejected by the signature
  itself (`TypeError: expected str`). `Timestamp.to_period` was already
  correct. This does not settle the `MonthBegin` question in GH-60671.
- The holiday observance table said `next_workday` "move[s] Saturday and
  Sunday to Monday"; it always advances at least one day, so a Monday
  moves to Tuesday. Fixed both rows and the two docstrings.
- The parser-engine section listed `on_bad_lines` and `decimal` as
  pyarrow-unsupported (they are supported), listed `verbose` (removed in
  3.0), and omitted `na_filter`. Replaced with a table regenerated from
  `_pyarrow_unsupported` / `_python_unsupported` and checked cell by cell
  against all three engines. `float_precision` is left out as deprecated,
  and `lineterminator` is python-unsupported.
- The `sep` and `engine` entries in the `read_csv` / `read_table`
  docstrings and in io.rst promised a `sep=None` fallback to the python
  engine that no longer happens, and claimed only pyarrow is
  multithreaded. The missing fallback is a 3.0 regression, reported
  separately as GH-66639; the docs here describe what actually happens.
- The crosstab-style `fill_value` type on the flex ops was `float or
  None`, though any scalar works. Applied @rhshadrach's suggested type
  and description to all 36 blocks (22 in `series.py`, 14 in `frame.py`).
  Note `DataFrame.eq`/`ne`/`lt`/`gt`/`le`/`ge` do not take `fill_value`,
  so they are untouched. This supersedes #66371 and #66634.

**Behavior that was correct but undocumented**

- `converters` are applied to the raw text before missing-value
  detection, so an empty field arrives as `''` and `na_values` is ignored
  for that column.
- `read_excel` silently loses a data row when a `MultiIndex`-column file
  lacks the separator row that `to_excel` always writes; mirrored into
  the `read_excel` and `ExcelFile.parse` docstrings.
- `read_sql` `chunksize` does not reduce peak memory without a
  server-side cursor; documented with a `stream_results` example.
- `ewm(adjust=False)` renormalizes weights across a missing value, so the
  documented recursion does not reproduce the result across a gap.
- Converting a nullable array to NumPy keeps `pd.NA`, so elementwise
  comparison raises; `to_numpy(na_value=...)` is the fix (GH-62802).
- `read_xml` silently ignores `stylesheet` when `iterparse` is used,
  since XSLT needs the whole tree in memory (GH-58857).
- `coerce_float` can silently round an integral `Decimal` above `2**53`.
  `read_sql_table` already warned about this; `read_sql` and
  `read_sql_query` now match (GH-61667).
- `read_excel` `usecols` ignores element order, matching what `read_csv`
  already documents (GH-61386).

thread in place of an API addition: repeating rows/columns via
`Index.repeat`, vectorized start/stop range expansion, splitting events on
interval boundaries, chunk-wise filtered reads (replacing a stale link
whose accepted answer used `.ix`), quoting fields containing the

`at_time`/`between_time` section.

title: BUG: BusinessDay added to a datetime64 array wrapped or landed on NaT (GH#66552)

labels.name: Missing-data
labels.description: np.nan, pd.NaT, pd.NA, dropna, isnull, interpolate

body:
One code path from GH-66552 (with the `n` truncation from item 3 of GH-66549, since it lives in the same two functions). Neither issue is closed by this — both cover many more sites.

`BusinessDay._shift_bdays` added the day shift with a raw `val + (7 * weeks + days) * DAY_PERIODS` inside a `nogil` loop. Two ways that went wrong:

```python
dti = DatetimeIndex([Timestamp(iNaT + 86400 * 10**9)])
dti + BDay(-1)          # -> [NaT];  dti[0] + BDay(-1) raises OutOfBoundsDatetime
date_range("2000-01-03", periods=1, unit="ns") + BDay(2**31 - 1)
                        # -> 2017-05-15, wrapped past int64
```

The shift now goes through `checked_mul`/`checked_add` and rejects a result equal to `NPY_NAT`, raising `OverflowError("Overflow in int64 addition")` past the `nogil` block — the same exception the neighbouring array ops already raise from `add_overflowsafe`. `NaT` inputs still pass through untouched.

`periods`, `weeks`, `days` and `_adjust_ndays` also held `n` in a C `int` while `_n` is `int64_t`, so a multiple of `2**32` was silently a no-op (GH-66549):

```python
dti = DatetimeIndex(np.array([946857600], dtype="M8[s]"))   # 2000-01-03, a Monday
dti + BDay(2**32)
# before: 2000-01-03 (unchanged)
# after:  16464909-06-25
```

Widening these is also what makes the two `checked_mul` guards live — with a 32-bit `weeks` neither product could overflow int64. The scalar `_apply` shared the truncation but was unreachable in practice: `timedelta(days=...)` caps out around `n ≈ 7e8` and raises first.

Checked the large-`n` results against `7 * (n // 5) + n % 5` days by hand, and swept 83 values of `n` across all 14 starting weekdays confirming the array and scalar paths agree exactly.

title: BUG: Week offset added to a datetime64 array wrapped or landed on NaT (GH#66552)
body:
One path from the GH-66552 inventory: adding a `Week` offset to a datetime64 array.

`Week._apply_array` has two branches and both were doing the arithmetic unchecked. The unanchored branch built the shift through a Python `timedelta` and then did a raw numpy `+`; the anchored branch (`_end_apply_index`) held `n` in a C `int` and did the add inside a `nogil` loop. Three symptoms, all verified pre-existing on `main`:

```python
# 1. sum fits in int64 but *is* iNaT, so it is indistinguishable from missing
>>> pd.DatetimeIndex([Timestamp(iNaT + 7 * 86400 * 10**9)]) + pd.offsets.Week(-1)
DatetimeIndex(['NaT'], dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq=None)

# 2. wraps, where the equivalent Timestamp op raises OutOfBoundsDatetime
>>> pd.DatetimeIndex([Timestamp.max]) + pd.offsets.Week(1)
DatetimeIndex(['1677-09-28 00:12:43.145224191'], ...)

# 3. n truncated to 32 bits -> silent no-op (GH-66549, item 3)
>>> dr = pd.date_range("2000-01-03", periods=1, unit="s")
>>> dr + pd.offsets.Week(2**32, weekday=0)
DatetimeIndex(['2000-01-03'], dtype='datetime64[s]', freq=None)   # == Week(0)
```

(1) and (2) now raise `OverflowError("Overflow in int64 addition")` — what `DatetimeIndex + Day(7)` and `DatetimeIndex + Timedelta(days=7)` already raise, since with no `weekday` a `Week` *is* a multiple of `Day`. (3) now computes the correct shifted date.

The unanchored branch computes the shift in i8 with `checked_mul` and adds via `add_overflowsafe`; the anchored branch widens `n`/`weeks`/`days` to `int64_t` and gates the shift and the add on `checked_mul`/`checked_add`, deferring the raise out of the `nogil` loop through a flag. Both branches are fixed together because they are the same operation on either side of a `weekday is None` test — fixing one alone would trade the bug for a disagreement between `Week(3)` and `Week(3, weekday=2)`.

Two things worth flagging:

- The unanchored branch loses its raw-numpy fast path. On 1M elements, `dti + Week(3)` goes 0.77 ms -> 4.53 ms, which lands it exactly on `dti + Day(21)` (4.36 ms) — already routed through `add_overflowsafe` on `main`. So it is now the same cost as its neighbours rather than uniquely fast-and-wrong. The min/max fast path sketched in GH-66552's Performance section would recover all of these callers at once; that is a separate PR. The anchored branch is 15.72 -> 16.20 ms.
- With `n` widened, `Week(2**32)` on an array now *succeeds* where the scalar still raises `OverflowError: Python int too large to convert to C int` — the scalar `Week._apply` goes through `timedelta(weeks=k)` and is capped by Python's 999999999-day limit. That is a scalar-only defect and not touched here.

`checked_add`/`checked_mul` get a third `cdef extern` declaration in `offsets.pyx`; hoisting all of them into a shared `.pxd` is GH-66549 item 5 and left alone.

Still returning `NaT` or wrapping on the array path, left for separate PRs: `BusinessDay._shift_bdays` and tz-aware `Day` (the naive `Day` path already raises).

title: BUG: segfault reading from a closed read_csv reader (GH#66622)
body:
closes #66622

`TextFileReader.read` closes the reader whenever the engine raises, and `close` frees the C tokenizer's buffers (`stream`, `word_ends`, `line_start`, `line_fields`) while leaving `parser->lines` and friends intact. The next read therefore believed it still had buffered rows, skipped re-tokenizing, and dereferenced the freed pointers in `_convert_column_data`.

The failing `dtype=` conversion in the issue is only one way in — a raising `converters=` callable, a mid-file `ParserError`, an explicit `reader.close()`, or just leaving the reader's `with` block all crashed the same way, with no error involved in the last two.

`TextReader.read` / `read_low_memory` now raise `ValueError: I/O operation on closed file.` when the reader is closed, matching what `engine="python"` already does. Exhausting a reader also closes it, so `CParserWrapper` tracks that case separately and keeps raising `StopIteration` there — that also stops the post-exhaustion path from calling `_tokenize_rows` on the freed parser, which was reading through a dangling `source` pointer.

title: BUG: Timedelta mul/div by a whole-numbered float computed in float64 (GH#66551)
body:
closes #66551

`float64` carries only a 53-bit mantissa, so applying a float operand in floating point rounded results that `int64` represents exactly. `Timedelta.min` is `iNaT + 1`, which rounds down onto the `NaT` sentinel, and `Timedelta.max` rounds up out of the `int64` range:

```python
>>> pd.Timedelta.min * 1.0
NaT
>>> pd.Timedelta.max / 1.0
OverflowError: Python int too large to convert to C long
>>> (pd.Timedelta(2**53 + 1, "ns") // 1.0)._value
9007199254740992          # should be 9007199254740993
```

A whole-numbered float has an exact `int` equivalent, so route it to the `int` path that is already exact. The rule is applied uniformly to `*`, `/` and `//`, on both the scalar `Timedelta` and `TimedeltaArray`, so an integral float now behaves exactly like the equivalent `int` and the scalar and array paths keep agreeing. Non-integral floats, `inf` and `nan` are untouched and stay in `float64`.

Zero is exempt: it needs no exactness fix, and routing it to the `int` path would turn `Timedelta(4, "ns") / 0.0` into a `ZeroDivisionError` and `Series / 0.0` from `NaT` into a raise — the regression GH-66552 warns about. Zero-divisor behaviour is unchanged from main.

One user-visible message change: an overflowing `tdi * 2.0` now reports `"Overflow in int64 multiplication"` rather than `"Overflow in timedelta multiplication"`, because it takes the same path as `tdi * 2`. Two existing tests updated accordingly.

This is the last live item in GH-66551 — I re-ran every reproducer in that issue against this branch and they all behave as the issue asks. The remaining sentinel work is tracked in GH-66549 and GH-66552.

title: BUG: read_csv(sep=None) raises TypeError instead of falling back to the python engine

labels.name: Regression
labels.description: Functionality that used to work in a prior pandas version

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import io
import pandas as pd

pd.read_csv(io.StringIO("a;b\n1;2\n"), sep=None)
```

### Issue Description

`sep=None` asks pandas to sniff the separator with `csv.Sniffer`, which only the python engine implements. Up to and including 2.2.3, passing `sep=None` without an explicit engine fell back to the python engine with a `ParserWarning`, and passing `engine="c"` explicitly raised a clear `ValueError`. Since 3.0.0 the fallback is gone, and the option reaches the C parser, which fails on an unhandled `None`:

```
  File "pandas/_libs/parsers.pyx", line 481, in pandas._libs.parsers.TextReader.__cinit__
    if len(delimiter) > 1:
TypeError: object of type 'NoneType' has no len()
```

Behavior on `io.StringIO("a;b\n1;2\n")`:

| | 2.2.3 | 3.0.0 – 3.0.5, main |
|---|---|---|
| `sep=None` (default engine) | falls back to python + `ParserWarning` | `TypeError` |
| `sep=None, engine="c"` | `ValueError: the 'c' engine does not support sep=None with delim_whitespace=False` | `TypeError` |
| `sep=None, engine="python"` | works | works |

The `engine="pyarrow"` case is separate but worth fixing alongside, because it fails silently rather than loudly — it ignores `sep=None` and parses each line as one column:

```python
>>> pd.read_csv(io.StringIO("a;b\n1;2\n"), sep=None, engine="pyarrow")
   a;b
0  1;2
```

The cause looks like GH-58668 (`CLN: Remove deprecated read_csv(delim_whitespace=)`, 0fc033618c7). `_clean_options` previously had:

```python
if sep is None and not delim_whitespace:
    fallback_reason = "sep=None with delim_whitespace=False"
    engine = "python"
```

When `delim_whitespace` was removed, the whole branch was deleted rather than reduced to `if sep is None:`. `_clean_options` still handles the other python-only separator cases (`len(sep) > 1`, non-encodeable `sep`), so `sep=None` is now the only one with no branch, and `engine` stays `"c"`.

This also means the documentation is currently wrong: the `sep` entry in the `read_csv`/`read_table` docstrings and in the IO user guide both still state that with `sep=None` "the Python parsing engine ... will be used", which no longer happens.

### Expected Behavior

`sep=None` with no explicit engine should fall back to the python engine and emit a `ParserWarning`, as in 2.2.3 and as the docstring describes:

```python
>>> pd.read_csv(io.StringIO("a;b\n1;2\n"), sep=None)
   a  b
0  1  2
```

`engine="c"` with `sep=None` should raise a `ValueError` naming the unsupported option, consistent with how `skipfooter` and regex separators are reported. `engine="pyarrow"` should raise rather than silently return a single column.

### Installed Versions

<details>

Reproduced on 3.0.0, 3.0.5, and main (`3.1.0.dev0+1481.g1d6b36eb8ff`); works as documented on 2.2.3.

</details>

title: BUG: vectorized month and quarter offsets raised a bare OverflowError (GH#66549)

labels.name: Error Reporting
labels.description: Incorrect or improved errors from pandas

body:
Addresses the first half of item 2 of GH-66549. Leaving that issue open for its remaining items (applying the month and timedelta components of a composed offset in one pass, and the duplicated `checked_*` externs).

`shift_months`, `shift_quarters` and `SemiMonthOffset._apply_array` build their results with `npy_datetimestruct_to_datetime`, whose overflow check surfaced as a bare `OverflowError` naming a pandas C source line, where the scalar path raises `OutOfBoundsDatetime` naming the offending date:

```python
>>> pd.DatetimeIndex([pd.Timestamp.max]) + pd.offsets.MonthEnd()
OverflowError: Overflow occurred at .../pandas/_libs/src/vendored/numpy/datetime/np_datetime.c:512
>>> pd.Timestamp.max + pd.offsets.MonthEnd()
OutOfBoundsDatetime: Out of bounds timestamp: 2262-04-30 23:47:16 with frequency 'ns'
```

Each `nogil` loop is now wrapped so the `OverflowError` is re-raised as `OutOfBoundsDatetime`. `dts` still holds the unrepresentable result when the exception propagates out of the loop, so the message names the date and the resolution it overflowed:

```python
>>> pd.DatetimeIndex([pd.Timestamp.max]) + pd.offsets.MonthEnd()
OutOfBoundsDatetime: Out of bounds nanosecond timestamp: 2262-04-30 23:47:16
```

This covers `MonthEnd`/`MonthBegin`, `QuarterEnd`, `YearEnd`, `SemiMonthEnd`/`SemiMonthBegin` and `DateOffset(months=/years=)` (which routes through `shift_months`), at every resolution.

The diff is mostly the reindentation from the three `try` blocks — `git diff -w` is a much shorter read. No per-element work is added; a 1M-element `DatetimeIndex + MonthEnd()` is unchanged at ~23 ms.

body:
`ArrowExtensionArray` and `ArrowStringArray` fallback to NumPy, object dtype, or a Python loop silentlly in many places. Some of those can be fix within pandas, but some need upstream work in Arrow. It also has impacts on downstream libraries such as PySpark.

I'll update this tracker incrementally. Some of those are from preliminary investigation and will need a deeper look.

- [ ] investigate why numeric dtypes are slow comparing to Cython path. (Arrow)


## String
### Method Resolution Order Shadowing

- [x] #66335 
- [x] #66339
- [x] #66431
- [ ] split
- [ ] rsplit
- [ ] extract: rejects unnamed groups and `flags`

### Missing Arrow Path

# Arrow

## Missing Kernels

- [ ] modulo: https://github.com/apache/arrow/issues/28497, https://github.com/apache/arrow/issues/46901
- [ ] floordiv: https://github.com/apache/arrow/issues/39386
- [ ] No `cumulative_sum`/`_min`/`_max` for `decimal128` — the only reduction family decimal lacks
- [ ] No hash aggregates for `dictionary` or `duration` — only `count` works, so both take a per-group Python loop in pandas
- [ ] No `hash_sum` for `string` — `groupby.sum()` on string falls to a Python loop (31.9 ms vs 4.5 ms for `min` at N=200k)
- [ ] No `utf8_casefold` — `utf8_lower` is not a substitute (`"Straße"` → `straße`, Python gives `strasse`)
- [ ] No per-character translate kernel — `.str.translate` is a Python loop at object-dtype speed
- [ ] No all-matches regex — `extract_regex` returns the first match only, so `.str.findall` has nothing to build on
- [ ] `floor_temporal`/`ceil_temporal`/`round_temporal` wrap at ±2³¹ days on the *value* — #50675 guarded the multiple, not the value, and duration now inherits it

title: BUG: memory_usage missing the engine's object copy (GH#66593)
body:
Fixes #66593

`Index.memory_usage` adds `self._engine.sizeof(deep=deep)`, which reports the
hashtable and nothing else. For arrow-backed string dtypes `_get_engine_target`
hands the engine `vals.astype(object)`, so the engine also retains a distinct
pointer array and a full set of freshly boxed `PyUnicode` objects that
`_memory_usage` never saw. For object dtype that array *is* the Index's own
array, which is why the bug only shows up on the string dtypes.

The fix, in `Index.memory_usage`: when the cached engine's array is an
object-dtype ndarray that is not the array backing `self._values`, add its
`nbytes`, and at `deep=True` also `lib.memory_usage_of_objects` on it. The
identity check is what keeps object dtype and `string[python]`, where the engine
shares our array, from being double counted; the `dtype == object` check keeps
the masked and datetime engines, which hold an i8/M8 view of our own buffer, out
of it.

I left `HashTable.sizeof` alone. Making it honour `deep` would double count for
object dtype, where the strings are shared with the Index and already counted,
and the hashtable cannot tell which case it is in. The Index is the only layer
that knows.

Three existing tests encoded the old accounting and are updated:

- `base/test_misc.py::test_memory_usage`: its local `_is_object_dtype` claimed
  only `storage == "python"` strings have a deep component. That is now false for
  any string Index with a cached engine, which this test always has.
- `indexes/test_old_base.py::test_memory_usage_doesnt_trigger_engine`: the
  engine's copy is allocated when the engine is constructed, not when its mapping
  is populated, so the `==` becomes `>=`. What the test is actually about, that
  `memory_usage()` does not build the engine, is untouched.
- `extension/test_categorical.py`: constructing a `Categorical` leaves a cached
  engine on the categories Index, so `memory_usage(index=False) == nbytes` no
  longer holds. Overridden locally to drop that engine rather than weakening the
  shared assertion for every EA. That assertion is already only conditionally
  true on main: `pd.Categorical(list("abcdefghij")).categories.get_loc("a")` makes
  `Series(c).memory_usage(index=False)` return 402 against `nbytes` of 102.

## Verified

x86-64 Linux, CPython 3.11.15, numpy 2.4.6, pyarrow 25.0.0, built from this
branch. CPU only.

The issue's reproducer goes from a reported growth of 16908 kB to 65408 kB, which
is 16908 (hashtable) + 4000 (pointer array) + 44500 (boxed strings). Against RSS,
500k keys x 40 chars, engine build only:

| dtype | reported before | reported after | RSS delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| `object` | 16.9 MB | 16.9 MB | 17.0 MB |
| `str` | 16.9 MB | 65.4 MB | 70.3 MB |
| `string[python]` | 16.9 MB | 16.9 MB | 16.8 MB |

`object` and `string[python]` are unchanged, which is the point of the identity
check. The residual 65.4 vs 70.3 MB on `str` is pymalloc arena overhead from
allocating 500k `PyUnicode` objects.

New test `test_memory_usage_counts_engine_object_copy` fails on the parent commit
and passes here. Full suite: 217415 passed, 0 failed (the 383 errors are missing
`qapp` and `httpserver` fixtures in my container, all in `pandas/tests/io`).
pre-commit and `mypy 2.1.0` clean on the changed files.

## Not verified

PyPy (the `not PYPY` guard mirrors `_memory_usage` but is untested here) and
32-bit. My `PyUnicode` totals differ from the issue's because I am on CPython 3.11
rather than 3.13; the ratio matches. I did not separately measure the frame-level
example in the issue, though it routes through the same code path.

A `bool[pyarrow]` Index also gets an object copy, and `memory_usage_of_objects`
will over-count its boxed singletons. That over-count is pre-existing for any
object array of shared objects, so I left it alone. GH-58529's `MultiIndex` case
is also untouched.

Thanks to @jbrockmendel for the report, which pinned both mechanisms and the
exact line in `_get_engine_target`.

title: BUG: segfault on next() after a chunked read_csv chunk raised (C engine)
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import io

import pandas as pd

# column "b" has one non-numeric token, so converting the first chunk raises
data = "a,b\n" + "".join(f"{i},{'oops' if i == 5 else i}\n" for i in range(20))

reader = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(data), dtype={"b": "int64"}, chunksize=10)

try:
    next(reader)
except ValueError:
    pass  # invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'oops'

next(reader)  # <-- segfault
```

### Issue Description

If converting a chunk raises, the `TextFileReader` is left in a state where the
next `next()` / `get_chunk()` call segfaults instead of raising.

The exception from the first chunk is the expected one:

```
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'oops'
```

The second call crashes the interpreter. `faulthandler` puts it inside the
Cython `TextReader.read` call:

```
Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault

Current thread 0x00000001d8f81c40 (most recent call first):
  File ".../pandas/io/parsers/c_parser_wrapper.py", line 234 in read
  File ".../pandas/io/parsers/readers.py", line 1923 in read
  File ".../pandas/io/parsers/readers.py", line 1985 in get_chunk
  File ".../pandas/io/parsers/readers.py", line 1843 in __next__
```

Scope, from varying the reproducer (identical results on 3.0.5 and 2.3.3):

| variant | result |
| --- | --- |
| `engine="c"`, `chunksize=10` | **segfault** |
| `engine="c"`, `iterator=True` + `get_chunk(10)` | **segfault** |
| `engine="c"`, `converters=` raising on row 5 instead of `dtype=` | **segfault** |
| `engine="python"`, `chunksize=10` | raises `ValueError`, no crash |
| `engine="c"`, no `dtype=` (first chunk does not raise) | fine |

So it is specific to the C parser, and what sets it up is that a chunk raised
during conversion — `dtype=` is just a convenient way to trigger that, and a
raising `converters=` callable does it too.

Not a regression: reproduces identically on 3.0.5, on 2.3.3, and on a source
build of current `main`. Nothing string- or pyarrow-specific is involved — the
reproducer has no string column.

### Expected Behavior

The second `next(reader)` should either raise a Python-level exception or return
the remaining rows. Crashing the interpreter is never acceptable, and it is
particularly bad here because catching a per-chunk conversion error and
continuing is a natural pattern for a chunked read.

title: PERF: read_csv string columns, cutting per-column-chunk GIL work
body:
The pyarrow string fast path (`_string_pyarrow_utf8`) re-runs its own setup on
every `(column, chunk)` call, all under the GIL:

- two function-level imports (`import pyarrow`, `from ...string_arrow import ArrowStringArray`)
- the option lookups behind the target decision in `_string_convert` —
  `using_string_dtype()` plus a freshly constructed `StringDtype(na_value=np.nan)`
  just to read `.storage`
- `ArrowStringArray.__init__` / `ArrowExtensionArray.__init__`, whose type
  checks, `pc.cast` and `ArrowDtype` construction are all redundant when the
  arrow type is known by construction

This PR resolves the target once per reader, caches the pyarrow imports, type
objects and dtype instances at module level, and assigns the three attributes
the constructors set (`_pa_array`, `_dtype`, `_cache`) directly.

Chunking is `DEFAULT_BUFFER_HEURISTIC // table_width` rows, so the number of
these calls is roughly string-columns × chunks and grows quadratically with
width. **The win is therefore a function of column count, and narrow frames see
nothing** — worth being explicit about, since the common 10-column file is flat.

### Benchmarks

Paired binary-swap: both `parsers` extension modules built up front,
hash-verified, and alternated within a single session (order flipped each round)
to avoid cross-session drift. 6 rounds × 5 reads, median. High-cardinality
ASCII string fixtures, default dtype unless noted.

| fixture | serial | 4 threads |
|---|---|---|
| 400 cols × 40k rows | **0.903** | **0.786** |
| 120 cols × 100k rows | 0.973 | 0.944 |
| 10 cols × 1M rows | 1.002 | 1.002 |

i.e. noise.

been re-run since the follow-up commit.

- Resolving the target once per reader pins which path the parser takes at the
  first string column it converts. This is observable only with `chunksize` /
  `iterator=True`, where flipping `future.infer_string` or `mode.string_storage`
  between chunks previously moved one read on or off the fast path partway
  through. The pin is one-directional: when the target resolves to the object
  path, storage is still chosen downstream, per chunk. I think pinning is the
  better behaviour, but happy to move the cache if you disagree.

> Split out of GH-66152, which is now stacked on top of this PR. That one raises the default worker count to the physical core count and needs a policy discussion; this one does not.

The parallel `read_csv` path added in GH-64347 picks its default worker count as `min(os.cpu_count(), 4)`. `os.cpu_count()` reports the machine's CPUs, not the ones this process may actually use, so a default `read_csv` inside a container limited to one CPU (`docker --cpus=1`, a Kubernetes CPU limit) or under an affinity mask (`taskset`, a SLURM cpuset) spawns up to 4 parse threads onto that allocation.

This clamps the default to the tighter of the CPU affinity mask and the cgroup CFS quota (v2 `cpu.max`, falling back to v1 `cpu.cfs_quota_us`/`cpu.cfs_period_us`). The cap stays at 4, so the change can only ever *lower* the worker count relative to what is on main — nobody gets more threads than today. An explicit `mode.max_threads` still wins in either direction.

The detection lives in a new `pandas/compat/_cpu.py`. The inline worker-count block in `_read` moves to `_default_n_workers()` unchanged apart from the clamp, which makes it directly testable.

Its unit tests live in a new `pandas/tests/test_cpu.py`, mirroring `pandas/tests/test_optional_dependency.py` for `pandas/compat/_optional.py`; the `_default_n_workers` tests stay with the rest of the parallel-read tests in `pandas/tests/io/parser/test_parallel_read.py`.

No whatsnew entry: `v3.1.0` is unreleased, so the parallel path this refines has never shipped. The existing GH-64347 performance entry still describes the behaviour accurately.

Doc fixes ride along:
- `io.rst` said the parallel path needs a file "at least 50 MB"; `_PARALLEL_READ_MIN_BYTES` is 5 MB. This is wrong on main today, independent of the rest of the PR.
- `io.rst` presents its eligibility conditions as sufficient ("happens automatically when all of the following hold"). This PR makes that false — a process limited to a single CPU satisfies every bullet and still reads serially — so the list gains a worker-count bullet.
- That 5 MB threshold applies to the data section, not the whole file: `_can_parallelize_csv` checks `file_size` *and* `file_size - data_start`, so a 5 MB + 1 byte file with a header line is over the threshold and still ineligible. Corrected in `io.rst` and in `_can_parallelize_csv`'s own docstring.
- `io.rst` and the `mode.max_threads` option docstring now mention the availability clamp. The option docstring also no longer lumps Windows together with Emscripten: an explicit `mode.max_threads` re-enables parallel reading on Windows, but is ignored under Emscripten, which cannot spawn threads at all.

Two existing tests needed a fix rather than a port. `test_parallel_default_thread_cap` and `test_parallel_default_off_on_windows` both pin `os.cpu_count` but not the new availability clamp, so each would fail on a runner with fewer usable CPUs than it assumes — exactly the environment this PR targets. Both now stub `available_cpu_count`, so they measure the cap and the platform gate rather than the runner.

labels.name: Testing

body:
The chunked half of `test_string_fast_path_matches_object_path` used a single `chunksize=7` for every file. On the 10-row `test*` files that is two chunks, but on the 2097-row `load_log` and 1440-row `productsales` it is 300 and 206 chunks, each read twice (object path and fast path). Those 16 params accounted for most of the runtime, essentially all of it per-chunk fixed overhead rather than parsing.

Chunk size is now picked per file, taking the largest value that still lands chunk boundaries in all four positions the parser distinguishes: starting mid-page, spanning a page boundary, falling wholly inside a data page, and a short final chunk. `load_log` goes to 250 (9 chunks) and `productsales` to 50 (29 chunks); the small files keep 7.

Coverage is unchanged. A larger size like 700/500 would be faster still, but at those sizes every chunk spans a page and the wholly-inside-a-data-page case disappears — the `test*` files do not cover it, since all 10 of their rows sit on the mix page. The four positions were enumerated per file at each candidate size to pick the values above, and a mutation check (corrupting the fast path's last string cell per chunk) confirms the comparison still fails on every file at the new sizes.

Locally 6.98s -> 2.28s for the test, with the slowest param going from 0.48s to 0.06s.
